strengths: Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks: state-of-the-art PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on RE10K (e.g., 31.57 PSNR with 8 views vs. 28.65 for the best prior method at 2 views), consistent cross-dataset generalization gains on ACID and DL3DV, and favorable runtime (0.025–0.03s reconstruction) and memory profiles (Tab. 1–4).

The decoupled design—compact, viewpoint-tied Gaussian representations refined via cross-attention against high-resolution image tokens plus low-cost self-attention—is a sensible and well-motivated architectural contribution that genuinely addresses the quadratic cost of full multi-view attention (Fig. 2 complexity analysis; Tab. 4 where DepthSplat OOMs while iLRM runs on a 4090).

Unusually thorough evaluation breadth for this area: varying view counts and resolutions, wide-baseline/wide-coverage settings (Tab. 5 vs. LongLRM and optimization-based methods), varying-overlap analysis (Tab. 10), same-Gaussian-count comparisons (Tab. 11), and training cost comparisons (Tab. 6).

Comprehensive ablations (Tab. 7–9, 12) that isolate each design choice (iterative refinement, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention, initialization), with plausible magnitudes of improvement for each component.

Clear writing with a well-structured method section, and supplementary material that covers implementation details, Gaussian parameterization, FLOPs calculations, and pose normalization, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Comparisons that use more input views than the baselines weaken the headline claims. In Tab. 1, the best prior result (Gen-Den, 28.65) uses 2 views while the strongest 'Ours' results use 4–8 views; a large fraction of the PSNR gain may come from the additional input information rather than the architecture itself. The apples-to-apples rows are Ours (2, F, F) = 28.65 vs. Gen-Den = 27.08, a much smaller margin than the abstract implies. The 4/8-view comparisons to DepthSplat are at least partially controlled (DepthSplat also trained with varying views in Tab. 3), but this should be stated more prominently.

The 'iterative refinement / mimicking optimization' framing is rhetorically strong but technically loose: there is no feedback loop from rendered output, no error signal akin to optimization residuals—each layer simply re-applies cross- and self-attention to tokens. The claimed analogy to per-scene 3D-GS optimization is more of a narrative device than a demonstrated mechanism; the ablation showing cross-attention at all layers helps is interesting but does not establish the optimization interpretation.

Fairness of some reported numbers is unclear: comparisons mix models trained with different iteration counts and hardware (e.g., Ours (2,F,F) trained 200k iterations vs. (4,H,F) at 100k; DepthSplat evaluated on different GPUs; the (4,H,F) ablation baseline in Tab. 7 is 29.24 while Tab. 1 reports 30.37 for the same configuration, presumably due to different training budgets—the discrepancy is not explained in the main text).

Rendering time is excluded from the timing comparisons while Gaussian counts differ across methods (Tab. 3), which can bias the reported wall-clock advantage; the paper should report end-to-end times or justify the exclusion more carefully.

The method requires accurate camera poses (Plücker embeddings) and remains pose-based, which limits practicality compared to emerging pose-free feed-forward models; this is acknowledged but bounds the impact.

Scalability of self-attention across viewpoint tokens remains a bottleneck for very large view counts (acknowledged in Limitations), and only up to 32 views are demonstrated—modest relative to the 'scalability' motivation.
GS-LRM, a key baseline, is marked as unavailable for re-evaluation, so some comparisons rely on numbers copied from prior reports rather than controlled re-runs.

strengths: The empirical evaluation is extensive: multiple datasets (RE10K, ACID, DL3DV), multiple viewpoint/resolution configurations, varying-baseline analysis (Tab. 10), and a same-Gaussian-count controlled comparison (Tab. 11) that isolates the benefit of the decoupled design.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial and concretely quantified: e.g., 0.19 sec vs 0.28 sec for LongLRM at 32 views (Tab. 5), OOM avoidance vs DepthSplat at 512x960 (Tab. 4), and large memory reductions (1.4 GB vs 5.87 GB in Tab. 3).

Ablation coverage is unusually thorough (Tabs. 6-9, 12), covering depth, iterative refinement, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention, group-attention, initialization, and mini-batch cross-attention, which strengthens the credibility of the design claims.
The scalability analysis (Fig. 2 complexity ratios, FLOPs derivation in appendix F) gives a transparent theoretical account of why the two-stage attention reduces cost.
weaknesses: The central 'iterative refinement' framing is conceptually overstated. The update blocks are simply stacked cross-attention/self-attention layers operating on fixed image tokens; there is no feedback from the rendered estimate (no re-rendering, no error signal), so the analogy to optimization-based 3D-GS refinement (Section 1) is rhetorical rather than mechanistic. The mechanism is closer to a standard deep transformer, and the alternating cross/self attention pattern is already established (e.g., VGGT, which the authors themselves concede in the appendix).

Comparison fairness is a recurring concern. In Tabs. 1 and 2, the headline 'Ours (4, H, F)' and '(8, H, F)' results use 4-8 input views while all baselines use 2 views; large PSNR gains (e.g., 31.57 vs 28.10 for GS-LRM) conflate architectural benefit with additional input information. Although a 2-view configuration is reported, the abstract and introduction claim general superiority based on the multi-view settings.

The model is large relative to its closest efficiency-oriented competitors (171-185M params vs MVSplat's 12M), and some baselines are omitted or weakened (GS-LRM marked as unavailable, Time reported as '-'; DepthSplat evaluated on a different GPU class in Tab. 4), making efficiency claims hard to verify uniformly.

Self-attention across viewpoint tokens retains quadratic complexity in the number of views (acknowledged in Section 4), which undercuts the scalability motivation that drives the paper; the framework 'scalability' claim is thus only partially delivered.

The mini-batch cross-attention scheme (Tab. 6) trades measurable quality (30.39 -> 30.08 PSNR) for compute, but the sampled-token schemes are heuristic and their effect on reconstruction stability or failure cases is not analyzed.

The paper requires ground-truth camera poses and normalizes scenes using extrinsics, limiting applicability relative to emerging pose-free feed-forward methods; this is acknowledged only as future work.

Writing/consistency issues reduce polish: a likely typographical hyperparameter (beta_2 = 0.095 in Appendix B), inconsistent notation between figures and text, and reliance on supplementary material for key details such as Gaussian decoding.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no explicit code release is stated in the manuscript (only a 'Project Page' link), and training requires substantial multi-GPU resources (8x H100/H200 for some configurations), which may hinder independent verification.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies concrete scalability bottlenecks (quadratic cost of full multi-view attention, resolution-coupled Gaussian density) in feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction, and each stated design principle (decoupling, two-stage attention, per-layer high-resolution injection) maps to a specific limitation.

Strong empirical results across multiple standard benchmarks (RE10K, ACID, DL3DV) and settings: e.g., 28.65 PSNR on RE10K at 2 views surpassing DepthSplat/GS-LRM, and substantial gains with more views (31.57 PSNR with 8 views) while remaining faster and more memory-efficient than baselines.

The wide-coverage comparison against optimization-based 3D-GS/Mip-Splatting and LongLRM (Table 5) is compelling: ~0.5s inference vs 13min optimization with comparable or better quality, and a practical finetuning recipe (Ours10/Ours50).

The scalability claims are supported by explicit complexity analysis (Fig. 2, Appendix F FLOPs calculations) and measured time/memory, not just architectural assertions; DepthSplat OOM at high resolution further substantiates the practical value.

Comprehensive ablations (Tables 6-9, 11-12) validate each component (iterative refinement, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, mini-batch cross-attention, self-attention role, initialization choices), including the informative same-Gaussian-count experiment (Table 11) that isolates the decoupling benefit.
Limitations are candidly discussed (self-attention bottleneck, dependence on known camera poses).
weaknesses: Comparison fairness: several headline results give the proposed method 4-8 input views while baselines use 2 views; although Table 3 and Table 10 show DepthSplat degrades with more views and the method improves, the magnitude of gains partly reflects the extra views, and a matched-view full-resolution baseline comparison is less prominent in the main text.

The 'iterative refinement mimicking per-scene optimization' framing is more of an architectural analogy (repeated cross-attention layers) than a demonstrated feedback loop; no explicit reconstruction-error-driven update is shown, and the paper does not compare against genuinely gradient-driven iterative methods (G3R, Gen-Den) in the wide-coverage or multi-view settings where the claim is strongest.

Some measured efficiencies exclude rendering cost, and training resource requirements are high (8 H100/H200 GPUs, curriculum schedules), which tempers the efficiency narrative and limits reproducibility for typical labs; code release status is not clearly confirmed beyond a 'Project Page' link.

Mini-batch cross-attention consistently trades quality for compute (e.g., 30.10 vs 30.37 PSNR in Table 1), and the 'ideal' random sampling scheme is dismissed for implementation reasons without deeper analysis; the contribution here is useful but incremental.

Presentation issues: Beta2 = 0.095 appears to be a typo (0.999?), Table 6 is referenced as 'Tab. 6' with details deferred to supplementary, and some ablation discussion refers to tables 'below' that are actually in the appendix, which slightly impedes readability.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and clearly articulated scalability problem in feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction: pixel-aligned transformer approaches incur quadratic cost in both view count and image resolution. The proposed decoupling of viewpoint tokens from image tokens, combined with per-view cross-attention and viewpoint self-attention, is a well-motivated design that demonstrably reduces cost (e.g., relative cost ratios 1:1:0.25:0.08 in Fig. 2) while maintaining reconstruction quality.

Experiments are comprehensive and convincing: comparisons against strong recent baselines (MVSplat, DepthSplat, Gen-Den, GS-LRM, Long-LRM) on RE10K, DL3DV, and cross-dataset generalization to ACID, plus wide-coverage settings (32 views, 540x960) where prior methods OOM or take minutes, while iLRM runs in ~0.5s with fewer Gaussians (1.4M vs 5.9M for DepthSplat in Tab. 4).

The supplementary material is unusually thorough: additional ablations (self-attention replacement, group-attention, initialization strategies), FLOPs analysis, geometry/depth evaluation via point-map metrics and CD/F-score, pose-perturbation robustness tests, same-Gaussian-count comparisons, and view-overlap stratified results. This materially strengthens the empirical case.

The ablations in Tab. 7 directly support the two core design claims: removing iterative cross-attention refinement or resolution decoupling each degrades performance, and token uplifting is validated in Tab. 7. Attention visualization (Fig. 8, Fig. 18) provides qualitative evidence that viewpoint tokens progressively align across views, consistent with the design motivation.
The method is honest about limitations (self-attention bottleneck, pose dependence, geometry fidelity), which is appreciated.
weaknesses: The 'iterative refinement' and 'optimization-as-inference' framing is more rhetorical than technically substantiated. The claimed analogy V(l) ≈ V(l-1) - η∇E(V(l-1); S) for cross-attention updates (and mini-batch cross-attention as SGD) is a heuristic interpretation, not derived or verified: no evidence is given that layers actually behave like gradient steps (e.g., no analysis of update magnitudes, no implicit objective recovered, no comparison to actual test-time or training-time refinement like G3R/Gen-Den which they distinguish themselves from). The contributions stand empirically, but the conceptual novelty may be thinner than the framing suggests.

The architectural ingredients are individually familiar: viewpoint/Plucker tokens with per-layer cross-attention to image tokens resemble alternating-attention designs in GS-LRM/VS-LRM and other latent-based models, and token uplifting is a standard upsampling mechanism. The novelty lies mainly in the specific combination and the efficiency analysis rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Some baselines are not strictly comparable: Gen-Den and GS-LRM are closed-source with numbers taken from prior reports; different training hardware/batch sizes are used for baselines in the same-Gaussian comparison (Tab. 17 acknowledges MVSplat/DepthSplat trained on H100 with smaller batches); the mini-batch cross-attention 'MC' variants are trained with 'equivalent computational budgets' whose definition is not precisely specified in the main text.

Scalability claims have an acknowledged ceiling: self-attention across viewpoint tokens remains O(N²), and Tab. 15 stops at 256 views where runtime (20.9s) grows quickly; a head-to-head comparison against sub-quadratic alternatives is deferred to future work. Also the method requires accurate camera poses, limiting applicability versus pose-free methods.
The paper does not state whether code will be released, which affects reproducibility given the detailed but complex training curriculum (multi-stage resolution, multi-GPU schedules) described.

Minor presentation issues: the gradient-descent interpretation in Sec. 'Token uplifting'/update block discussion should be clearly marked as intuition; Table 5 comparisons to Long-LRM involve fine-tuning protocols that could be described more symmetrically.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and timely problem: the quadratic cost of full attention over multi-view image tokens in feed-forward Gaussian splatting models, and the excessive number of pixel-aligned Gaussians generated by current methods.

The proposed design is sensible: decoupling a compact viewpoint-token representation from high-resolution image tokens, per-view cross-attention, token uplifting to bridge resolution mismatch, and mini-batch (subsampled) cross-attention together reduce memory and compute, as demonstrated in Fig. 2 and Tables 3-8.

Empirical evaluation is broad: RE10K, DL3DV, ACID cross-dataset generalization, wide-baseline zero-shot settings (Tanks&Temples, Mip-NeRF360), pose-perturbation robustness (Tab. 14), large-view-count inference scaling up to 256 views (Tab. 15), varying-overlap comparisons (Tab. 16), and a same-Gaussian-count controlled comparison (Tab. 17).

Ablations (Tabs. 6, 7, 9, 18) are reasonably thorough, covering layer depth, the role of iterative cross-attention vs. single cross-attention, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, and initialization choices.
Reported inference efficiency is impressive (e.g., 0.53s for 32 views at 540x960 vs. 8 minutes for per-scene 3D-GS optimization), and the qualitative results generally look competitive.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty. The core structure is very close to GS-LRM's alternating cross-/self-attention transformer; the main deltas are deferring Gaussian decoding to the last layer, using low-resolution viewpoint tokens, and subsampling cross-attention queries. Each component is a plausible engineering refinement rather than a new concept, and the paper does not clearly delineate what is fundamentally new beyond Fig. 2's complexity arithmetic.

The 'iterative refinement' / 'network-as-optimizer' framing is overclaimed. Unlike G3R or Gen-Den, which use actual rendering gradients, the update here is just stacked attention layers with residual connections applied to fixed image tokens; the gradient-descent analogy (Sec. 2.2 'Interpretation') is informal and not substantiated by any experiment. The claim of 'feedback-driven refinement' in the abstract oversells what is a standard transformer with deferred decoding.

The scalability story is internally inconsistent. The method still requires self-attention across all viewpoint tokens, which the authors themselves concede is the bottleneck in Sec. 5; Tab. 15 shows memory growing quadratically (20.9s at 256 views), and the headline of 'efficient and scalable' reconstruction is thus only partially realized. Also, per-view cross-attention cannot resolve cross-view ambiguities that only global image-token attention could.

Mini-batch cross-attention discards most image evidence at each layer (only quarter of tokens sampled), and image tokens are never updated across layers; the paper provides no analysis of failure modes or of whether subsampled tokens ever recover missed information, beyond aggregate PSNR deltas (~0.2 dB drop in Tab. 8).

The method depends on accurate ground-truth camera poses and static scenes, and reconstruction fidelity rather than geometry is the objective; these limitations are acknowledged but not quantified against pose-free or geometry-supervised alternatives, weakening the practical usefulness claim.

Some comparisons are potentially confounded: baselines on DL3DV are finetuned from RE10K checkpoints with different view-sampling protocols, and the strongest recent competitor (Long-LRM) is evaluated partly with re-implementations; differences in training data volume and schedule across rows of Tab. 5 are hard to audit.

Quantitative gains over baselines are modest at matched settings (e.g., ~0.4-0.9 dB PSNR over DepthSplat/Gen-Den on RE10K in Tab. 1), so the paper's main selling point rests on speed/memory, which the self-attention bottleneck limits.

Reproducibility concerns: training uses 8 H100s for 50k-200k iterations with multi-stage curricula, and key details (mini-batch sampling schedule, uplifting dimension k, supplementary-only FLOPs) are spread across the supplementary; no code release is mentioned.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: decoupling the scene representation (viewpoint tokens) from input images, with iterative refinement via per-view cross-attention, directly addresses the quadratic cost of full image-token attention in prior feed-forward 3DGS models (e.g., GS-LRM). The two-stage (cross-then-self) attention design with a compact viewpoint space is a sensible and well-argued solution.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning RE10K, DL3DV, ACID (cross-dataset), Tanks&Temples and Mip-NeRF360 (zero-shot), with multiple operating configurations (2/4/6/8/12/32/48 views, multiple resolutions). Tables report PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS alongside #Gaussians, inference time, and memory, which is the appropriate accounting for an efficiency-focused paper.

Thorough ablation studies: number of update layers (Tab. 6), iterative refinement vs. single cross-attention (Tab. 7), token uplifting, resolution decoupling (Tab. 7), alternative attention schemes including group-attention and self-attention replacements (Tab. 9), and initialization strategies. These are concrete and support the architectural claims.

The attention visualization (Fig. 8, Fig. 18) provides qualitative mechanistic evidence that viewpoint tokens progressively align to geometrically corresponding regions across layers, supporting the iterative-refinement narrative.

The supplementary material is substantial and addresses potential fairness concerns: same-#Gaussian comparison (Tab. 17), varying-overlap evaluation (Tab. 16), pose-noise robustness (Tab. 14), depth/geometric evaluation, and FLOPs analysis.
The paper is honest about limitations (self-attention bottleneck over many views, dependence on GT poses, geometry not explicitly supervised) in a dedicated section.
weaknesses: No explicit statement of code or model release. For a paper whose central contribution is an architectural recipe with several nontrivial implementation details (token uplifting, structured quarter cross-attention, pose normalization), reproducibility depends heavily on details that would be difficult to reimplement exactly.

The mini-batch cross-attention (quarter cross-attention) is a heuristic sampling scheme justified mainly by analogy to mini-batch gradient descent. The comparison to random sampling is asserted ('complicates efficient implementation') rather than empirically validated with a fair implementation; the theoretical gradient-descent interpretation (Sec. 'Decoding into 3D Gaussians' discussion) is loose and not experimentally substantiated.

Cross-method comparisons involve somewhat heterogeneous settings: baselines trained with different data, resolutions, and hardware (RTX 4090 vs. H100 for DepthSplats in Tab. 4; Long-LRM re-evaluated with different attention kernels). While the authors disclose this, some headline efficiency numbers (e.g., '0.5 seconds vs. 8 minutes') mix hardware and pipeline assumptions that weaken direct comparability.

The optimization analogy framing (each layer ≈ one optimization step) is evocative but not rigorously established; a stronger validation would compare against actual test-time per-layer feedback (e.g., G3R-style gradient feedback), which the authors defer to future work.

Self-attention over viewpoint tokens remains O(V²) in the number of views, so the scalability claim is partial: gains at 128–256 views (Tab. 15) come from a still-quadratic term, and the wide-coverage results at 32 views rely on finetuning/finetune-from-Long-LRM protocols rather than a single fixed model, complicating interpretation of generalization claims.
Dependence on ground-truth camera poses limits applicability to real in-the-wild capture, which is acknowledged but not addressed even in a preliminary form.

Some presentation issues: the notation (V, H, F) is dense and takes effort to parse; Table 5 mixes in-house finetuning variants (Long-LRM_i0) with zero-shot variants, making the strongest claims (40/48-view rows) rest on a comparison against a method the authors themselves retrained/re-evaluated.
